Tat antibodies from HIV-1-infected individuals or SHIV-infected macaques can be divided in two main subsets, depending on the epitope recognised.
Tat antibodies from vaccinated animals and from SHIV-infected macaques are able to recognise and neutralise the cognate Tat protein and to inhibit the Tat-induced apoptosis of human T cells.

the identification of Tat-specific antibodies that may be used as a therapeutic tool in AIDS patients.
the identification of antibodies able to block Tat activity, and the study of their potential role in the control of HIV-1 infection.
the development of a vaccine based on Tat protein and the identification of Tat antibodies that could be used as a diagnostic tool or as an immunotherapeutic reagent.

Tat antibodies from vaccinated monkeys and HIV-infected patients can be divided into several categories, some of them with the capacity to recognise the cognate protein and inhibit its biological activity.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Tat antibodies from vaccinated or SHIV-infected animals have the capacity to recognise and neutralise Tat protein and might have the potential to be developed into a therapeutic agent.

Tat antibodies from long-term non-progressor HIV-infected individuals, from immunised rabbits and from SHIV-infected macaques have the potential of interfering with the biological activity of Tat and might be of interest for vaccine design.

the Tat protein is a very complex protein with a large number of epitopes, and that antibodies against Tat might play a significant role in the control of HIV infection.
